extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, law students, and litigants concerned with patent-infringement damages and accounting
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and legal rules for measuring and proving damages and accounting for profits in patent-infringement cases (including law vs. equity remedies, jury assessment, and allowable deductions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of actual damages
rubrics_metrics.description: "By the terms 'actual damages, sustained by the plaintiff,' are meant such damages as he can actually prove, and has in fact sustained, as contra-distinguished from mere imaginary or vindictive damages..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actual damages must be damages the plaintiff can actually prove and has in fact sustained; they are not speculative or vindictive. Where actual damages are established, the court may, under statute, treble them (up to three times the verdict) according to the circumstances of the case (Act of July 4, 1836; Act of July 8, 1870, §55/§59).

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure for infringement by use: defendant's actual profits during illegal use
rubrics_metrics.description: In cases of infringement by actual use (e.g., making and using a patented machine) give the value of such use during the time of the illegal user — i.e., the amount of profits actually received by the defendant, but not profits they might have made by reasonable diligence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the infringer actually used or sold machines, one mode is to assess the defendant's profits from that use. The jury must consider only profits actually received, not hypothetical profits the defendant might have earned with reasonable diligence. The plaintiff may also add losses to which he was subjected by the piracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recovery limited to damages during period of infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Where no established patent or license-fee exists, general evidence of utility may be submitted to the jury to estimate damages, 'not for the whole term of the patent, but only during the continuance of the infringement.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A recovery of such damages does not vest in the infringer the right to continue the use; the jury should confine calculation to the actual time of illegal use and the losses suffered during that time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jury may weigh multiple ingredients in estimating damages
rubrics_metrics.description: The price of the machine, the nature, actual state and extent of the use of the plaintiff's invention, and the particular losses to which he may have been subjected by the piracy are proper ingredients to be weighed by the jury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have often preferred leaving the subject open to the jury to estimate actual damages 'according to the circumstances of each particular case' rather than prescribing a single universal rule. Examples and case citations (Pitts v. Hall; Seymour v. McCormick) illustrate discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between defendant's profits and patentee's lost profits
rubrics_metrics.description: Damages may be measured by either (a) profits the plaintiff derives from his own manufacture/sales, or (b) profits the infringer derived from the use of the invention; neither measure is universally controlling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The measure of defendant's profits is not controlling where those profits do not correspond with the fair profits the patentee would have realized; juries may look to what the patentee would have made under the circumstances if left alone, but such a claim must be substantiated by clear and distinct evidence (Seymour v. McCormick).

rubrics_metrics.name: Actual damages must be proven with evidence; otherwise nominal damages only
rubrics_metrics.description: If the plaintiff rests his case after merely proving an infringement, he is entitled to nominal damages, but no more. Actual damages must be calculated, not imagined, and an arithmetical calculation cannot be made without certain data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiff bears burden to furnish evidence sufficient for a jury to assess damages; absence of price or value evidence (e.g., license price) will make large damage verdicts unsustainable (City of New York v. Ransom).

rubrics_metrics.name: When part of the claimed invention is not original (improvements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where part of an invention is not original (e.g., patent is for an improvement), that part cannot be mixed with original parts so that the jury may regard the whole as a unit when estimating damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Damages must reflect only the contribution of the patented improvement; the patentee cannot treat an old element as if it were newly patented to claim a larger recovery (Jones v. Moorehead).

rubrics_metrics.name: Price of the machine as a measure of damages — limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Some have maintained that the price of the invented machine is a proper measure of damages when piracy occurs by making and using the machine, but this measure has significant objections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court criticism: using price as measure effectively forces a sale of the exclusive right (compelling patentee to 'sell' his right) and ignores circumstances where patentee never sold rights or value depends on limited users; courts caution against universally applying price-as-measure except where plaintiff consents or circumstances justify it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verdict does not vest infringer with right to continue use
rubrics_metrics.description: A recovery of damages for the period of infringement does not vest in the infringer the right to continue the use of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if damages equal price for use, that does not automatically transfer the patent right or allow ongoing infringement; courts distinguish remedies and rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difference between cost and sale price is not all profit — necessary adjustments
rubrics_metrics.description: The difference between the actual cost of making a patented machine and its sale price is not all profit; the jury must take into account interest on the capital, risk of bad debts, and expenses of selling to arrive at the defendant's real profits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Profits should be computed as a manufacturer would: receipts minus payments, including reasonable deductions (interest, bad debts, selling expenses). Courts require these adjustments to avoid overstating profits (Wilbur v. Beecher).

rubrics_metrics.name: Counsel fees are not proper element for jury damages in patent cases
rubrics_metrics.description: It has been decided by the Supreme Court that counsel fees are not a proper element for consideration by the jury in estimating damages for infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counsel fees should not be included in jury-calculated damages (Day v. Woodworth; Teese v. Huntingdon).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-1870 election of remedies; post-1870 ability to recover both profits and damages in equity
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior to the Act of 1870 a patentee elected between equity (profits) and law (damages). The Act of July 8, 1870 changed the rule so both profits and damages may be recovered in equity, and courts may grant injunctions and assess damages under equitable principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 55 and 59 of the 1870 Act allow suits in equity to recover profits and damages, and permit courts to increase damages up to three times the jury verdict; actions must be brought during the patent term or within six years after expiration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial discretion to treble damages (statutory enhancement)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a verdict is rendered for the plaintiff the court may render judgment for any sum above the amount found by the verdict as the actual damages (not exceeding three times the amount), according to the circumstances of the case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court's exercise of discretion to increase damages should be guided by the nature of the infringement — e.g., wanton piracy and unjustified conduct may justify trebling; mere assignee speculation does not. Judges have explained factors and provided examples (Leavitt, J.; Schwarzel v. Holenshade).

rubrics_metrics.name: In accounting for profits, defendant cannot claim salary paid to himself as deductible
rubrics_metrics.description: In an accounting for profits the defendant cannot be credited with a sum of money as a salary earned by and paid to himself while engaged in the business producing the profits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowing defendants to reduce recoverable profits by paying themselves 'salaries' would permit infringers to evade liability; courts treat such self-payments as gains unless bona fide and reasonable (Williams v. Leonard).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equitable measure of profits: difference between cost and yield; allowable deductions
rubrics_metrics.description: In equity the profits to be accounted for are computed and ascertained by finding the difference between cost and yield; in estimating cost take into account price of materials, interest, expenses of manufacture and sale, and bad debts, and nothing else.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The computation mimics a manufacturer's profit accounting: receipts minus necessary payments. Deductions allowed: market value of materials on hand at start, cost of materials subsequently acquired for the infringing business, expenses of manufacture and sale, rents, interest, usual salaries of managing officers, repairs, purchase of new machinery, tools, and fixtures. Disallowed: extraneous deductions, disguised dividends as salaries, and (in some cases) wear and tear/depreciation (Rubber Co. v. Goodyear; Livingston v. Woodworth). The aim: prevent the wrong-doer from profiting by the infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Master may refuse allowances that disguise profits (e.g., extraordinary salaries, improper deductions)
rubrics_metrics.description: A master accounting may refuse to allow extraordinary salaries shown to be dividends disguised as salaries, refuse value allowances for materials bought for purposes of infringement, and refuse to allow profits due to elements not patented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Masters must scrutinize bookkeeping and deny allowances that conceal profits; courts have approved refusal to allow such deductions where credible evidence shows concealment or where allowances would credit non-infringing elements (Rubber Co. v. Goodyear).

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure of profits for process patents or partial improvements: advantage attributable to the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: For an improved process (or improvement in part of a machine), the proper measure of the defendant's liability is the advantage the defendant derived from using the complainant's invention over other processes then open to the public, not the entire profits of the manufacture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court asks what advantage in cost, skill, convenience, or marketability the invention provided compared to other available methods; profits attributable to that advantage are the recoverable amount. If other adequate processes existed, the defendant is not liable for entire profits (Mowry v. Whitney; Jones v. Morehead).

rubrics_metrics.name: When manufacture was ordered before notice of patent, only nominal damages may be proper
rubrics_metrics.description: If defendants manufactured patented articles on an order given by a third person and partially executed before notice of the patent, and only a small number were made after notice, nominal damages only may be proper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timing of notice to the defendant and the number of infringing units after notice affect damages; courts have reduced recoveries to nominal where most activity occurred before knowledge of patent (Bryce v. Dorr).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee's market-established license value fixes actual damage ceiling
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the patentee has established the market value of his improvement as separate and distinct (e.g., by selling licenses at a set price), that license price fixes the average of his actual damage when the invention is used without his license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If patentee claims more than established license value, he must substantiate by clear and distinct evidence to recover above that amount; jury instructions should reflect that established license values are controlling absent clear evidence to the contrary (Seymour v. McCormick).
